lead: Oximetry reads oxygen saturation from the colour of pulsating blood. Two light-emitting diodes, red at about 660 nm and infrared at about 940 nm, shine through a finger. A photodiode measures what passes. The pulsatile part is separated from the steady tissue part, and their ratio gives SpO₂. Impedance pneumography watches breathing from the small rise in chest impedance as air enters the lungs. An apnoea monitor alarms when that change stops for 10-20 s. These three measurements sit together at the bedside.
prereq: You need: breathing volumes and flow from Chapter 2.5 and Chapter 2.6, and bridge circuits and bio-amplifiers from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Pulse oximetry: two wavelengths and one ratio

blocks.text: Pulse oximetry rests on the Beer–Lambert law: absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length; the light that gets through falls exponentially with both.

blocks.where: A is absorbance (no unit); ε is the molar absorption coefficient at that wavelength, in litre per mole per centimetre (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹); c is concentration (moles per litre); d is path length (centimetres). The units cancel, so A has no unit.

blocks.text: In a finger, light crosses skin, bone, venous blood and arterial blood. The steady part is DC. Each heartbeat pushes arterial blood into the finger, so the light path through arterial blood lengthens and shortens; this small changing part is AC. The AC is the pulsatile arterial signal.

Oxygenated and reduced haemoglobin absorb differently. At red 660 nm, reduced haemoglobin absorbs more. At infrared 940 nm, oxygenated haemoglobin absorbs more. Two wavelengths therefore separate oxygen saturation from the total amount of blood and tissue in the path. A red LED and an infrared LED are switched on alternately, often several hundred times per second. One photodiode on the far side measures the transmitted light for each wavelength.

items: Switch the red and infrared LEDs alternately.
Convert the photodiode current to a voltage and separate the two wavelength channels.
Split each channel into DC by low-pass filtering and AC by band-pass filtering at the heart rate.
Compute the ratio R from the two channels.
Read SpO₂ from an empirical calibration table or curve.

blocks.where: AC<sub>red</sub> and AC<sub>IR</sub> are the pulsatile amplitudes in the red and infrared channels (same light units); DC<sub>red</sub> and DC<sub>IR</sub> are the steady levels (same units); R is dimensionless.

blocks.text: R rises as saturation falls. The machine converts R to SpO₂ through an empirical calibration curve, built by measuring R in volunteers at known saturation. In one common table, R = 0.55 reads about 98%.

sections.h3: What pulse oximetry cannot tell you

blocks.text: SpO₂ is a percentage: oxygenated haemoglobin as a share of oxygenated plus reduced haemoglobin in arterial blood. Carboxyhaemoglobin and methaemoglobin are not counted as reduced haemoglobin, which is why they push the reading in the wrong direction. It is not a measure of breathing. A patient on oxygen can have a normal SpO₂ while breathing badly and retaining carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is seen by capnography or blood gas; apnoea is seen by chest movement or airflow. Saturation alone cannot detect either. This is the central limit of pulse oximetry.

items: Motion: probe movement changes the light path; the AC looks like a pulse and R becomes wrong.
Low perfusion: a cold finger, shock or low blood pressure makes the arterial AC small; noise dominates.
Nail polish and ambient light: dark polish absorbs red and infrared; strong room light adds a steady offset.
Carboxyhaemoglobin: carbon monoxide poisoning makes haemoglobin absorb red light like oxygenated haemoglobin, so SpO₂ reads falsely high.
Venous pulsation and severe anaemia can also mislead; the displayed value is SpO₂, not arterial SaO₂ from a blood sample.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call oximetry an extra bedside measurement rather than a core one; with ECG, blood pressure and respiration it completes the set.

Impedance pneumography uses the chest as a conductor. Air is a poor conductor, so when the lungs fill, transthoracic impedance rises. Two or four electrodes are placed on the chest. A small alternating current, about 50 kHz, is passed between a pair of electrodes; another pair measures the voltage. The current is kept small for safety. The impedance change is roughly 1 Ω per litre of air in a typical adult.

A bridge circuit converts the small impedance change into a voltage. A band-pass amplifier keeps the breathing frequency and rejects drift and the ECG. The output is a respiration waveform: up on inspiration, down on expiration. Chest movement and the cardiac stroke add artefacts; the cardiac stroke is a small bump at the heart rate on top of the breathing wave.

blocks.where: S is sensitivity (ohms per litre); ΔZ is the impedance change (ohms); ΔV is the volume change (litres). A 0.5 Ω change with a 0.5 L breath gives S = 1 Ω per litre.

blocks.text: An apnoea monitor watches this waveform. It sounds an alarm when no impedance change larger than a set amount occurs for 10-20 s. It is used for neonates in hospital and at home. A threshold that is too low alarms on cardiac artefact; too high misses shallow breathing.

figure.caption: Two light-emitting diodes shine through the finger, the photodiode measures transmitted light, and the pulsatile-to-steady ratio becomes a saturation reading. The ratio shown is 0.55, which maps to about 98%.

spec.title: Pulse oximeter signal path
spec.aria: Two light-emitting diodes shine through the finger, the photodiode measures the transmitted light, and the pulsatile-to-steady ratio of the two channels is converted to a saturation reading.

examples.question: A finger probe gives red channel DC = 100 units and AC = 2 units, infrared channel DC = 110 units and AC = 4 units. (a) Compute R. (b) The calibration table maps R = 0.55 to about 98%; which way does R move if saturation falls? (c) An apnoea monitor shows a 0.5 Ω impedance change with a 500 mL breath; find its sensitivity.
steps: Less oxygenated blood absorbs more red light, so the red AC/DC term grows; the infrared term falls; R rises and the table reads a lower SpO₂.
S = ΔZ / ΔV = 0.5 Ω / 0.5 L = 1 Ω per litre.
examples.answer: R = 0.55, so the table reads about 98%; a fall in saturation raises R; the monitor sensitivity is 1 Ω per litre.
examples.check:
red_dc = 100.0
red_ac = 2.0
ir_dc = 110.0
ir_ac = 4.0
R = (red_ac / red_dc) / (ir_ac / ir_dc)
sens = 0.5 / 0.5
print(round(R, 2))
print(round(sens, 1))

traps: A normal SpO₂ does not prove good breathing. A patient on oxygen can hypoventilate and retain carbon dioxide while the saturation looks fine.
R rises as saturation falls. Do not invert the ratio or read the calibration table backwards.
AC is the pulsatile arterial part; DC is the steady tissue, bone and venous part. Swapping them destroys the measurement.
The figure 1 Ω per litre is a typical adult value, not a fixed constant. Electrode position, chest shape and lung volume change it.
Carboxyhaemoglobin and nail polish can make SpO₂ falsely high or low. Motion and low perfusion make the ratio noisy, not just the waveform ugly.

quiz.q: Which two wavelengths does a pulse oximeter use, and which haemoglobin does each favour?
quiz.a: Red at about 660 nm, where reduced haemoglobin absorbs more; infrared at about 940 nm, where oxygenated haemoglobin absorbs more.

quiz.q: Why separate each channel into AC and DC before taking the ratio?
quiz.a: DC carries skin, bone and venous blood; AC carries pulsatile arterial blood. The ratio cancels the steady path and leaves the arterial colour change.

quiz.q: A probe gives red AC/DC = 0.03 and infrared AC/DC = 0.05. Find R and say whether the table reads above or below 98%.
quiz.a: R = 0.03/0.05 = 0.60. This is higher than 0.55, so the table reads a lower saturation.

quiz.q: A patient on oxygen has SpO₂ = 98% but has stopped breathing. Explain how both statements can be true.
quiz.a: Oxygen in the blood can stay high for a short time while ventilation stops. SpO₂ measures saturation, not airflow or carbon dioxide. Apnoea needs chest movement, airflow or capnography.

quiz.q: Why does impedance pneumography use a small alternating current at about 50 kHz instead of DC?
quiz.a: AC avoids electrode polarisation and allows a safe small current. The measurement is of impedance change, not resistance alone.

quiz.q: How long without a set impedance change usually triggers an apnoea alarm?
How does motion artefact produce a false SpO₂ reading?
quiz.a: Motion changes the light path and creates an AC-like signal. The ratio then mixes arterial pulsation with movement, so R and the table output become wrong.

quiz.q: A 400 mL breath gives a 0.8 Ω impedance change. Find the sensitivity in Ω per litre.
quiz.a: 0.4 L breath gives 0.8 Ω, so S = 0.8/0.4 = 2 Ω per litre.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern pulse oximeters add motion rejection and low-perfusion algorithms, but the ratio-of-ratios idea remains the base. Reflectance probes read the forehead or oesophagus when fingers are cold or poorly perfused. Overnight oximetry is used in sleep apnoea screening, and impedance respiration appears in wearable vests and home apnoea mats. Search terms: ratio-of-ratios calibration, reflectance pulse oximetry, transthoracic impedance respiration.
